claims.text: The specific oxygen affinity of the added element governs protective-oxide formation and long-term stability above 900 °C.
Crystallographic and thermal-expansion compatibility between the oxide and substrate governs oxide-scale stability.
Al additions to CrFeCoNi promote formation of Al2O3.
Si additions to CrFeCoNi promote formation of SiO2.
Al2O3 or SiO2 scales on these alloys grow slowly and coherently.
Al2O3 or SiO2 scales adhere well and resist thermal-cycling stresses.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNi alloys form fast-growing mixed Mn-based oxide phases.
Poor crystallographic and thermal compatibility of Mn-based oxides with the substrate generates high residual stresses.
Residual stresses in Mn-based oxide scales cause crack initiation and spallation.
Mn mobility and depletion can produce pores and accelerate oxide growth in CoCrFeNiMn alloys.
The initial material is CrFeCoNi in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
The intervention is a controlled addition of Al, Si, or Mn to CrFeCoNi.
The proposed exposure consists of isothermal oxidation above 900 °C for tens to hundreds of hours in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
Al- and Si-alloyed samples will have more adherent, more slowly thickening scales with fewer defects than the baseline and Mn-alloyed samples.
Mn-containing samples will exhibit rapid oxide growth, increased defect density, cracking, and spallation.
CrFeCoNi without an added X element is the experimental baseline.
Phase structure and microstructural evolution may affect oxide growth rates, stresses, and defect densities during long-term exposure.
Failure of the Al- and Si-alloyed samples to outperform the Mn-alloyed and baseline samples in scale growth, defect density, coherence, and spallation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
